One windy autumn evening in Paris, I was sitting in silence with my friend C, Auguste Dupin in his small library, which was dark. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly the door opened, and in walked Monsieur G, the Prefect of the Paris police, an old acquaintance of ours. <break time="0.8s" /> Dupin rose to light a lamp, but he sat down again when the Prefect said he wanted advice about an official matter. <break time="0.8s" /> If it is a problem that requires thought, said Dupin, we shall examine it better in the dark. <break time="0.8s" /> The Prefect explained that the case was very simple but very odd, and Dupin replied, Perhaps the mystery is a little too plain. <break time="0.8s" /> At this the Prefect roared with laughter, crying that nobody had ever heard of such a foolish idea. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, having made us promise to keep it secret, he told us that a letter of great importance had been stolen from the royal apartments. <break time="0.8s" /> The thief, he said, was the Minister D, a bold, clever man, who was now using the letter to gain power over its owner.

A royal lady had been reading the letter in her room when another important person, from whom she wished to hide it, suddenly entered. <break time="0.8s" /> Failing to push it into a drawer, she left it open on the table, with the address on top. <break time="0.8s" /> The Minister D, came in, and he at once noticed the letter, recognized the handwriting, and guessed her secret from her nervous face. <break time="0.8s" /> Laying a similar letter of his own beside it, he later took hers, and she dared not stop him with the other person present. <break time="0.8s" /> Hoping to get the letter back, the Prefect had searched the Ministers house every night for three months, the Minister being often away. <break time="0.8s" /> His men had opened every drawer, drilled into the legs of every chair, and examined each page of every book in the house. <break time="0.8s" /> Twice the Minister had even been stopped by fake robbers and searched, but the letter was nowhere to be found. <break time="0.8s" /> When Dupin said the Minister was no fool, the Prefect answered that he was a poet, which he thought was nearly the same thing. <break time="0.8s" /> Dupins only advice was to search the house again thoroughly, and the Prefect left us, looking more unhappy than I had ever seen him.

About a month afterward, the Prefect paid us another visit and admitted that, although he had searched the house again, he had found nothing. <break time="0.8s" /> The reward had become very large, he said, and he would gladly give fifty thousand francs to anyone who could help him. <break time="0.8s" /> In that case, said Dupin calmly, you may write me a check for that amount, and I will hand you the letter. <break time="0.8s" /> The Prefect sat speechless for some moments, staring at my friend with his mouth open, as if he could not believe his ears. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, after several long pauses, he signed the check, and Dupin, unlocking a desk, took out the letter and handed it over. <break time="0.8s" /> The Prefect seized it with wild joy and, his hand trembling, glanced at it before rushing out without a single word. <break time="0.8s" /> When he had gone, Dupin explained that the Paris police were skillful in their own way, but their methods did not suit this man. <break time="0.8s" /> He then told me about an eight year old schoolboy who was famous for always winning a marble game called even and odd. <break time="0.8s" /> Before each guess, the boy would make his face look like his opponents, and he would notice what thoughts arose in his own mind.
